scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The spiral dance was first performed in Berkeley, California, during a 1979 ritual intended to meld art, music, and politics, as well as celebrate the publication of Starhawk's book The Spiral Dance.
It grew into a central ritual for Reclaiming Witches and an annual Neopagan tradition in the United States, particularly as a Samhain celebration to honor the dead and celebrate rebirth.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed to raise power in a ritual, emphasize community, and mark occasions such as Samhain to honor the dead and celebrate rebirth.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers hold hands in a single line and follow a designated leader using a grapevine step.
The leader moves counter-clockwise to form an inner spiral.
Upon reaching the interior of the circle, the leader turns around to lead the line clockwise while facing the incoming dancers.
Watch for Grapevine line step, The Center Turn.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Starhawk, author of the 1979 book The Spiral Dance, whose publication launch ritual established the dance tradition.

Variants depend on circle size and intimacy: close-knit circles may incorporate a kiss exchanged between passing dancers, whereas large public rituals discourage kissing to maintain structural rhythm.
Developed within 1970s feminist Wicca and the Reclaiming movement in California as a ceremonial group ritual.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The Spiral Dance is a Neopagan ritual practice used to raise power and honor the dead. Intimacy customs like kissing depend on participant consent and circle norms; rhythm and boundary respect should be maintained.
